headline: A Priest's Faith in Children Built India's Largest Student Environmental Movement
meta_description: Father Robert Athickal showed how trusting young people with real responsibility could transform local tree-planting into a movement reaching hundreds of thous…
summary_short: A Jesuit priest in Patna believed children could do serious environmental work. His trust turned schoolchildren's tree-planting into India's largest student environmenta…
body:
When Father Robert Athickal first encountered a small group of schoolchildren in Patna worried about trees being cut around their crowded city on the Ganges, he recognized something adults often miss: that young people could be trusted with serious work. For nearly four decades, he proved that belief right. Starting in 1988 with just students meeting after class and traveling by bicycle to spread their message, Athickal helped build Tarumitra—meaning "Friends of Trees"—into one of India's largest student environmental movements, eventually reaching hundreds of thousands of young campaigners across schools and colleges nationwide.

Tarumitra's early success came from practical simplicity. Student groups cleaned neglected plots, planted roadside gardens, and transformed garbage dumps into what they called "Oxygen Belts." These projects required no specialist equipment or large budgets, making them easy for schools everywhere to replicate. By giving students real responsibility—representing the movement at meetings, organizing school units, leading demonstrations—Athickal showed that environmental education meant more than learning about problems. It meant actively solving them. When the Jesuits provided ten acres at Digha near Patna in 1994, students between ages 12 and 15 planted what became a biological reserve holding hundreds of tree and plant varieties, including species disappearing from northern India.

Athickal wove together Indian philosophy and Catholic theology into his environmental vision. He spoke of "universal cousinship"—drawing on the Sanskrit concept vasudhaiva kutumbakam, the world as one family—to argue that humans had moral obligations toward animals, plants, rivers, and soils. His ashram-style reserve became a place where ecological ideas met daily life: students observed how soil, insects, and plants connected while eating food grown without synthetic chemicals. Though he received awards and an honorary degree, most of Tarumitra's work continued through ordinary school groups addressing problems in their own communities, proving that trust in young people yields slow but deeply rewarding results.
quick_facts: Founded Tarumitra in Patna, India in 1988 with just schoolchildren
Movement eventually reached hundreds of thousands of student campaigners
Established 10-acre biological reserve at Digha planted by children ages 12-15
Combined Jesuit teaching with Indian philosophy on environmental responsibility
Gained UN consultative status and sent youth to international gatherings
